title: Winter thaw days did not decrease next-summer peak NDVI of pan-Arctic tundra in 1982-2022 at 0.5-degree scale; a rare-thaw signal depends on three regional events and a Nordic positive control failed
abstract: Question: do winter warm events (thaw days) decrease the greenness of Arctic tundra in the next summer, as the Arctic browning hypothesis states? Data: PKU GIMMS NDVI v1.2 (consolidated 1982-2022, AVHRR-only 2001-2015), CRU TS 4.09, NCEP/NCAR Reanalysis 1 daily Tmax, and GHCN-Daily stations. Method: 3,076 tundra cells (0.5 degree; warmest month 0-10 C), QC-screened June-August peak NDVI; November-March thaw days (Tmax above 0 C); controls for summer warmth of this and the previous year and summer rain; cell and year effects; errors clustered by year and spatial block. The plan was written before the regressions. Results: 10 more thaw days changed peak NDVI by +0.0005 (95% CI -0.0011 to +0.0021), while a 1-SD cooler summer gave -0.0025 (t = 4.4). North America and Eurasia in 1982-2001 and 2002-2022 gave four point values from +0.0001 to +0.0034. Region-year effects, cell trends, other exposure measures, June NDVI, no QC screen and the previous winter gave no clear decrease. R1 thaw-day anomalies followed 23 stations (r = 0.71), and station thaw days also gave no decrease (+0.0020, CI -0.0004 to +0.0045). A dummy for 5 or more thaw days in normally frozen cells gave -0.0073 (CI -0.0125 to -0.0021), but it came from three region-years (Baffin-Nunavik 2011 and 1986, Chukotka 2007), became -0.0038 (CI -0.0108 to +0.0033) with region-year effects, and no single event was outside its placebo-year range. The positive control failed: the documented Nordic 2012 browning after the record December 2011 thaw was not visible (2012 rank 28 of 41 from low). Conclusion: at this scale, winter thaws do not explain year-to-year tundra peak greenness; summer warmth does. Limitations: coarse reanalysis exposure, 1/12-degree half-month maximum NDVI that missed a documented event, few rare events.
